items.title: Agents Acting Safely on Our Behalf
items.summary: What happens to the web when the ones browsing it are no longer people? Sarah Drasner , Area Tech Lead at Google , sits down with us ahead of her Agentic Web keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America. She works through that question from both directions: rebuild the web so agents can use it properly, or build agents smart enough to handle the web as it already exists. We get into the split between computer-use and browser-use agents on one side and API and MCP agents on the other. We also watch a real example of the idea in action: an agent pulling speaker photos from Flickr, hunting down company logos, and loading everything into Canva so the human only touches the creative part. From there, Sarah shares the unlikely origin story of WebMCP (and who's to blame for it). We then pressure-test a bold idea: a WebMCP gateway that could cover the huge share of websites that will never ship support on their own. Along the way, we cover the instinct that separates senior engineers, the ability to sense which business problems are actually worth solving. We also talk about how thought experiments cut through a pile of competing priorities, the hacky WebMCP workarounds already showing up in the wild, and why the best agent experiences are the ones that delight customers in ways they never saw coming. In fact, AI may be changing what should be considered foundational knowledge that all students must learn. items.title: AI Is Coming for Tasks Before It Comes for Jobs
items.summary: Neil Thompson on What Workers Actually Think, Why Big Firms Win, and Where the Human Still Fits. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast • Pocket Casts • YouTube • AntennaPod • Podcast Addict • Amazon • RSS . MIT FutureTech director Neil Thompson joins Ben Lorica to discuss how AI is reshaping work, the economy, and the future of automation. Drawing on recent research, Thompson explains why AI’s impact on most occupations may unfold gradually rather than arrive as a sudden shock, why adoption continues to lag behind technical capabilities, and why the fixed costs of implementation favor larger firms. They also explore the future of entry-level jobs and professional training, the changing economics of consulting, emerging AI safety risks, and whether open-weight models will eventually dominate inference. So today we welcome back Neil Thompson, director of MIT’s FutureTech Research Project, who was last on the podcast in the year of COVID, October 2020. So Neil, welcome back to the podcast. Neil Thompson. It’s my pleasure to be here. Ben Lorica. So I guess before we start, give us a one sentence, one to two sentence description of the future tech project. Neil Thompson. Yeah, so we are a we’re a research group that is sits both within the computer science AI Lab and the Sloan School of Management, both at MIT, were one of MIT’s largest research groups. We got more than 100 people, and we’re quite unusual in that we’re about half computer scientists and half economists. And so we try and think both about technically what’s going on and how you can put that into big models so that we know how it’s going to affect people, how it’s going to change growth, those kind of big questions, and at some some deeper level, you know, if we think broadly about the things we do, we think about what’s driving AI progress, what effects it’s going to have, and then we also do some work specifically on AI risk, which, as you can imagine, has been a lot in the last week or so. Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah. All right. So the reason I have Neil back is they have a couple of really interesting papers that caught my eye. But when Neil was last here, we talked about a paper they released at the time on the computational limits of deep learning . So maybe let’s go quickly and score that paper . I guess six years after the fact, so I guess one of the things that it got right early was the cost pressure, right? So around chips, capital, electricity, things like that, right? So let’s let’s stay on the positive side of the ledger, first. So, what are the things you feel that paper got right? Neil Thompson. Yeah. So, I think what you said is right. I think we were we were on the right side of it in terms of saying like this seems like one that the scaling laws are one of the main drivers, and I think indeed that you know has has been true, and that meant that we were going to progress from systems that were really not that expensive to systems that were very expensive, and where that cost pressure was going to be important. And of course, now we’re really seeing that, right? We see these systems where all of a sudden people are like, “Ah, maybe don’t use the most advanced system for these things. So I think that’s one of the things we got right. I think another thing we got right, but didn’t call enough, is when we actually did the economic modeling of this, we implicitly put in some terms for algorithmic progress, right? And we were people were really not talking about algorithmic progress in that we sort of we had had measured in that, but we really didn’t know sort of what was going on there. We really didn’t call it out very much, and I think it was just stuff that we people in Epoch and a few other places did over these the coming years to say, oh, let’s actually call that out and realize how important that is. So I think those were sort of the two things that we got right. I also have one big thing we got wrong, which if you want to make that turn yet,. Ben Lorica. Yeah. So on the on the algorithmic on the algorithmic progress, I guess you folks kind of hinted at it at a high level, as you mentioned. But obviously, on the specifics, like you know, now we’re using mixture of experts, maybe quantization, distillation, and so on, right? So, but at least you kind of hinted that’s probably going to happen just because of pressure. Neil Thompson. Yeah. So, so we I mean we knew that algorithmic progress was going to happen you know had to happen. Like we said that pressure was there, but we actually implicitly, if you actually look at the regressions we ran where we were trying to estimate how fast these models were improving, we put in effects that said over time you might be able to get more out of it, and so we were actually implicitly already measuring that. But as I say, like the problem was we didn’t know exactly what was the thing that was going on there, so we didn’t really call it out at that point. But what’s clear is you can even go back to that thing and you can see that it’s actually a very substantial number, and so this is you know I think that’s turned out to be something you know you gave a couple of examples of it of course by far the biggest example was transformers when they came out but those are the kind of things where you’ve seen suddenly we can harness every additional you know GPU much more effectively that’s made a big difference and particularly made a big difference for the biggest models that people use. So it, you know, calls a C library that sorts a list or something like that, and it doesn’t actually have to sort that list itself. And so we sort of we sort of finally got into it, but we were imagining that would be more of a heart of how AI was trained, and now it’s really more like AI has just been trained in a very broad way, and now we have it learning to use tools, and they can now learn to use those tools efficiently. Ben Lorica. Neil Thompson on What Workers Actually Think, Why Big Firms Win, and Where the Human Still Fits.

MIT FutureTech director Neil Thompson joins Ben Lorica to discuss how AI is reshaping work, the economy, and the future of automation. Drawing on recent research, Thompson explains why AI’s impact on most occupations may unfold gradually rather than arrive as a sudden shock, why adoption continues to lag behind technical capabilities, and why the fixed costs of implementation favor larger firms. They also explore the future of entry-level jobs and professional training, the changing economics of consulting, emerging AI safety risks, and whether open-weight models will eventually dominate inference.

Neil Thompson. So you know the short the short answer is that we do see adoptions lagging significantly behind the capabilities, and I think there are sort of two reasons for this. So you can imagine the dentist. We keep talking about right. That dentist has just looked in this person’s mouth, right? They’ve just done all these things. Like usually, only later that they write in stuff in the medical record, and actually it might not even be everything that they write in. The other thing, of course, is just that in practice, it takes a bunch of effort to adopt AI, right? This is not. I mean, you know, even even if it’s something as simple as just calling in calling the API, you have to you know set that up, make sure that it’s going to be reliable, and of course, it can go you know significantly more difficult than that as you build an agent pipeline, you build Markdown files, you’re building, et cetera, et cetera, to make it all work together, and so all of those things can carry costs, and we think that friction exists. And so what we do see is right now something like half of the potential. It looks like about half the potential gains that you would get from adopting this are sort of eroded by all of these other costs that you’re having to pay, and that’s what seems to be like slowing down the benefit that people are getting, but we do see very substantial drops from year to year, and so that you know it seems like as as I think as you would expect, as people build better tools, better platforms in order to make AI easier to implement, more and more people using it as they build it. The stuff that people are already using that helps it as well.

Ben Lorica. So, so the desire is there. It’s just that the infrastructure or the pipe data pipelines or whatever this are not yet in place. But assuming they’re in place, people are willing to adopt.

Neil Thompson. So, so I mean, we certainly do see adoption, and we see adoption moving pretty quickly. There are, of course, other challenges as well. So economists have, for a long time, you know, I think their response to computer scientists who say this is all going to happen, pardon me, this is all going to happen incredibly quickly, is to say, well, that may be true, but we know in general, lots and lots of processes have bottlenecks, and if you automate a part of the process, something else can become a bottleneck. And so, you know, I’ve had many, many discussions, for example, with people who run software engineering organizations, right? And they say, “Hey, it’s amazing how much more code we can write, and it’s amazing how frustrating it is for our senior people who have to review code because they’re getting lots and lots of stuff in there where people are people who don’t know better are just handing them stuff and like yeah that’s pretty good, and to give to give you a sense of the scale of this, so Mert Demirer and some co-authors did some work at MIT recently, and they showed that when Claude Code and some of these other tools come out, you get something like an 800% increase in the amount of lines of code written, and then you get many, many fewer like you still get an increase, but much, much smaller increase in the number of commits that people are doing, the number of files that are created, etc. To the point where, if you actually look at like real releases into the world, it goes up 20% So from 800% to 20% right, and that’s really telling you something is going on there, where like there are bottlenecks that mean that you produce lots more lines of code, but maybe they’re not as good ideas, maybe they don’t fit in as well. You’re not able to sort of leverage it in the same way you were, and hence you don’t get all of that flow through. And so yes, moving fast, but there is this sort of diminution that happens.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, very similar to the mathematician’s observation of generation is cheap, verification is getting easier, but the acceptance and validation in the analog and software would be deployment is not keeping pace. Neil Thompson. So, so I mean, it also it is also empirical in the sense that we’re going to ground it. But yeah, I mean, I think the biggest contribution here is theoretical. I agree with that.

Ben Lorica. And so, so give us a give us a high level description of the findings.

Neil Thompson. Sure. So broadly, what the world we’re in for this paper is worth thinking about. Okay, once AI starts to replace tasks in the economy, how fast does it happen, and what does it mean for the world? Okay. Now, the this is a this type of model is something called a general equilibrium model in economics, and this is one where you don’t just simply say, well, you know, software demand for software developers changed. That means their wages change, or something like this. The general equilibrium means that like different people might choose to use software, different people might move into software as the wages change, and everything has to rebalance before things come out. Okay, and so this is you know really what macroeconomists think about when they think about managing the whole economy, and it’s particularly important if you think about something like AI, which is going to have very broad effects across a lot of things. Fine, but of course, under those circumstances, like you might have had to pay a fixed cost for that machine, and that’s not usually something that is in these in these models that people have written down. Neil Thompson. Very much so. Exactly,.

Neil Thompson. Exactly, right. And so this is, and you know, because we do see this big difference between large firms and small firms, it definitely suggests that there’s something like this going on. I think you talked to you know you talked to lots of firms. We did you know I can’t remember if it was I think something like 30 case studies before we wrote the sort of antecedent to this paper, and we saw again and again people saying oh actually you know gathering the data was a really big part of this right lots of the lots of the cases the off the shelf system can do a bunch of stuff but it actually doesn’t have the stuff you really need within a firm because you say, “Well, we have all these products, and that’s never been part of any training set that these that the AI models have used. Ben Lorica. So, so in any kind of new technology trend, it seems like you have a stereotype for which sectors and which industries will move first, right? So, I see financial services, maybe, right? So, so in the case of AI, for some reason, legal seems to have moved first, right? So, are the are the sectors that we perceive to be the most AI aware now in two years or three years? Will they will we still have that perception?

And then are the same firms going to lead? And I think for the first one, I think the answer is probably yes. That said, you know it’s certainly possible that in some of these areas, like using AI well in that area is going to require expertise, right? It’s going to require maybe even maybe even a.

Ben Lorica. Specialized maybe a specialized model even.

Neil Thompson. Exactly, and so those kind of things might push it to be like that role is different. You say, well, you know, you need to adapt to this particular system. You know, nobody in your industry has that level of expertise. We’ll parachute that person in, right? Ben Lorica. So in closing, you mentioned safety at the top that your lab works on safety. That’s why there’s people who are pushing new ideas, post transformers, or there’s people working on world models or multimodal models, right? So, so it seems to me that P Doom. I don’t know if my P Doom has got gotten higher over the last few weeks. What about you?

Ben Lorica. Cyber is I think something that to be to be taken. Right,.

Neil Thompson. The level of coordination, the level of like you know, we AIs are all in one boat. Let’s you know figure out how to do this in a sort of collective. Yeah, yeah. You can you can imagine.

Neil Thompson. Right, exactly, yeah, exactly. So, I mean, exactly. I think already today we should be worried about cyber stuff, right? The bigger question for me is, what are the people inside the lab seeing in the very cutting edge most model in terms of biological risk or something like this, right? Ben Lorica. Yeah so. several things can be true at once, right? One, AI will probably allow people to write even more secure software, right? Because they can run even more rigorous tests. Neil Thompson. Exactly right so there I could buy the argument that it would be open weights. I think the for me the biggest question mark there is if you think about distillation, right? Because we were able to distill, and that means that, from the point of view of customers, either we have better models for the same price, or our models can be run at you know 30% less than the other models. Then you could imagine the proprietary models providers actually be the ones who win, and so that-that to me is the biggest question. I think right now the data supports the way you just argued it, but I’m not-I’m not sure. I feel confident that will necessarily be true going forward. So that’s the question mark to me.

Ben Lorica. Yeah. By the way, the shift is already happening, right? So open models are starting to handle more and more of the inference, and the ecosystem around the open models continues to grow. In terms of,.

Neil Thompson. I mean, you know, we’ve we’ve looked at, for example, the applications in science, and there’s, if anything, it’s actually going the other way. So proprietary models are gaining share in the applications in science. So to me, unsure, but yeah, I can imagine trends in both ways.

Ben Lorica. Yeah, yeah. and also, I mean, there’s there’s just lots of arguments in favor of open models in terms of customization control, you know, controlling your roadmap and destiny, right? And being able to customize and not having anyone else look at your data, right? So, oh,.

Neil Thompson. And I have had many, many discussions with people where the very first question they ask as they start down this road is, “How can I make sure nobody else gets to see my data? Right.

Ben Lorica. And by the way, the cloud providers, the hyperscalers, cloud providers, all of these people benefit. The more competition there are for models, the more people use AI. So, I mean, Nvidia is just announced they’re going to continue investing in Nemotron, right? So, right, and.

items.title: Your Ranking Model Is Optimizing the Wrong Thing with Zoe Weil - #780
items.summary: In this episode, Zoe Weil, co-founder and CEO of Sequen, joins us to discuss how ranking systems can use live behavioral signals to optimize for purchases rather than clicks or search relevance alone. Zoe explains why approaches developed at data-rich social platforms don’t necessarily translate to retailers and how Sequen uses scroll speed, hover duration, and other in-session interactions to infer shopper intent without relying on user identity. We explore the company’s large event models and its architecture of specialized models that transform streaming events into features for downstream rankers. Zoe describes the infrastructure required to serve dynamic rankings within milliseconds, why the team chose Rust for its backend, and how evaluation harnesses connect model improvements to business outcomes. We also discuss the tradeoffs between advertising and organic revenue, continuous model improvement, and the boundary between useful personalization and surveillance. 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/780 .

In this episode, Jeff Witt, Global Process Digital Authority at GE Vernova, examines why industrial AI demands a different standard of rigor than its enterprise counterpart, from edge computing architectures to context-rich recommendations frontline workers can trust immediately. He also outlines a framework for earning the right to automate, proving a process is documented, optimized, and consistent before scaling AI across multiple sites. This episode is sponsored by Poka. Learn how to evaluate AI vendors by assessing leadership expertise, and why funding benchmarks can signal product maturity and stability.
